Hoodlum
HOOD-lum
noun (Silent Generation slang)
American, of uncertain origin; first recorded in San Francisco around 1870 for the gangs of young toughs there, and the many stories told of its source remain unproven. By the 1940s and 50s it was the everyday word, often shortened to hood, for the leather-jacketed street tough and the juvenile delinquent of newspaper headlines.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1955 a hoodlum was the young tough on the corner — ducktail haircut, switchblade in his pocket, trouble in his eye — the kind of boy mothers warned their daughters about. Scripture knew the type three thousand years earlier. Solomon’s first counsel to his son is about the gang on the corner: "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). The hoodlums say, come with us, there is easy money and excitement; the father answers, "My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path" (Pro 1:15). "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men" (Pro 4:14). The first psalm blesses the man who will not walk, stand, or sit with them (Psa 1:1). So a grandfather must be plain: stay away from the hoods. But Scripture will not let us stop there. Christ has a way of saving hoodlums. A thief crucified beside Him heard, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luk 23:43). Paul wrote to a church full of former thieves and drunkards: "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified" (1Co 6:11). The Christian keeps his children from the hoodlum’s path, and prays for the hoodlum, too.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, from San Francisco about 1870; an everyday 1940s–50s word) for a street tough — and Scripture both warns the young away from such company (Pro 1:10) and shows Christ saving such men (1Co 6:11).

HOODLUM, n. (American, c. 1870; everyday 1940s–50s; short form hood) A young street tough; a ruffian; a petty criminal. "Stay away from that pool hall — it’s full of hoodlums."

Decode for families: a hoodlum is a street tough or a young criminal — a crowd to stay away from, and a person to pray for.

Key Scripture

Pro 1:10 — "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not."

Pro 1:15 — "My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path:"

Pro 4:14 — "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men."

Luk 23:43 — "And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise."

1Co 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

Modern Corruption

A plain word for a real danger; the only caution is that it can become a label that writes a young man off, when Christ has saved many hoodlums.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong in naming hoodlums for what they are. Violence, theft, and intimidation are sins, and Proverbs opens with a father warning his son against exactly this company. Parents of the 1950s who used the word were often right to worry.

The caution is in how the word is used. It was sometimes thrown at any boy with long sideburns or a poor family, and a label can harden a child into what he is called. Scripture judges by deeds, not haircuts, and it never treats any sinner as beyond reach (1Co 6:11). A Christian family can keep its children out of the gang and still hope and pray for the boys in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Of uncertain origin → San Francisco hoodlum (c. 1870, young street toughs) → American everyday word → 1940s–50s hood, the juvenile delinquent.
